title: Scientists Trace Avocado Flowers' Daily Sex Switch to a Single Gene 44 Million Years Old
excerpt: A team of University of California researchers has identified the gene behind one of botany's oldest puzzles — why avocado flowers flip between male and female phases on a precise daily schedule.
body:
• A single gene called SDMYB controls whether avocado trees flower as female in the morning or afternoon, determining their A-type or B-type classification.
  • The gene has been maintained by natural selection for 44 million years and is found in at least 26 non-avocado species within the laurel family.
  • The discovery could help breeders develop molecular markers to predict a tree's flowering type years before it blooms, cutting the current 5-to-8-year wait.
  • True cinnamon, a close relative that uses a similar mating system, appears to have evolved the trait independently — suggesting nature invented this trick more than once.

A century-old mystery about why avocado flowers switch between male and female phases every day has been solved by a team of scientists across five University of California campuses. Their study, published as a preprint on bioRxiv, pins the trait to a single gene called SDMYB — and shows that nature has been running this genetic clock for at least 44 million years.

Avocado trees produce hermaphroditic flowers, but each bloom opens twice over two days. In "A-type" cultivars such as the commercially dominant Hass variety, flowers open as female — receptive to pollen — in the morning, then close and reopen as pollen-shedding males the following afternoon. "B-type" trees run the opposite schedule, opening female in the afternoon and male the next morning. The system, called heterodichogamy, forces cross-pollination between the two types and has shaped avocado cultivation for thousands of years.

The Gene Behind the Clock

Led by Jeffrey S. Groh of UC Davis and Graham Coop, also of UC Davis, the research team mapped the flowering dimorphism to a genomic region on chromosome 10 containing SDMYB, a transcription factor belonging to the R2R3 MYB family. A dominant version of the gene confers A-type flowering, according to the study. The dominant allele contains changes in conserved functional domains that create a phase delay in its expression rhythm, pushing the second flowering opening later in the day — matching the delayed schedule seen in A-type trees.

"Haplotypes at this locus form an ancient trans-species polymorphism maintained by negative frequency-dependent balancing selection over 44 million years."

— Groh et al., bioRxiv preprint

The gene's link to circadian jasmonate signaling — a hormonal pathway plants use to track time of day — explains how the daily rhythm stays so precisely synchronized. Earlier genome-wide association studies had narrowed the search to a 20-kilobase region on chromosome 10, but this is the first study to identify the specific gene and its evolutionary history.

An Ancient Polymorphism Shared Across Species

What makes the finding remarkable is the gene's age. The two versions of SDMYB — one conferring A-type and the other B-type flowering — have persisted side by side for 44 million years, maintained by a form of natural selection called negative frequency-dependent balancing selection. When one type becomes too common, the rarer type gains a pollination advantage, keeping both versions in play across evolutionary time.

The researchers found the same SDMYB variants in at least 26 non-avocado species within the Lauraceae family, which includes bay laurel, camphor, and sassafras. Some of those species had not previously been known to use this mating system at all, suggesting the gene's influence extends far beyond the avocado grove.

Cinnamon's Parallel Path

One of the study's more surprising findings involves true cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum), a fellow member of the Lauraceae that uses a strikingly similar daily sex-switching system. Yet cinnamon lacks the SDMYB polymorphism entirely, suggesting it evolved the same reproductive strategy through a completely different genetic route — a textbook case of convergent evolution within a single plant family.

What It Means for Growers

The practical implications are significant. Avocado trees take five to eight years to reach maturity, and a single tree can produce more than one million flowers per season, of which fewer than 0.1% set fruit. Knowing a tree's flowering type at the seedling stage — through a simple genetic test rather than years of waiting — could streamline breeding programs and help growers plan orchards with the right mix of A-type and B-type trees for optimal pollination.

Molecular markers based on the SDMYB gene could also accelerate efforts to breed varieties better suited to new growing regions, an increasingly urgent priority as climate change shifts the boundaries of avocado-friendly territory. India, now the world's seventh-largest avocado producer, has seen rapid expansion in states like Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, and Maharashtra, where matching pollination partners is critical for yield.

What's Next

The study, funded by the National Institutes of Health, involved researchers from UC Davis, UC Riverside, UC Irvine, UC San Diego, and UC Berkeley. The team plans to investigate how the SDMYB gene interacts with environmental cues such as temperature, which can disrupt the normally rigid flowering schedule — a phenomenon well documented in cooler growing regions where the daily rhythm breaks down and partial self-pollination occurs.

The preprint has not yet undergone formal peer review, but the breadth of genomic, evolutionary, and expression data it presents has already drawn attention from plant geneticists worldwide. For a fruit that generates roughly $14 billion in global trade annually, cracking the genetic code behind its peculiar reproductive clock carries both scientific and commercial weight.
